findings.title: Locked funds
findings.description: The buy() function allows users to attach a deposit that exceeds the required price, but the contract does not refund the excess amount. This lack of refund logic results in the excess funds being permanently locked within the contract balance. The cause is the absence of a check and refund mechanism after verifying that the attached deposit meets or exceeds the price. An attacker could exploit this by intentionally overpaying to lock funds, though the primary impact is on user experience and fund accessibility rather than direct theft. The impact includes loss of user funds due to inability to retrieve overpaid amounts, leading to reduced trust and potential financial loss.

findings.title: No check for promise results
findings.description: In the resolve_purchase() and resolve_offer() functions, the contract initiates token transfers via promises without verifying their success. The root cause is the lack of error handling for cross-contract calls, particularly when transferring funds to the owner and treasury. An attacker could exploit this by forcing a failed transfer (e.g., via a malicious receiver contract), causing the system to assume payment succeeded while funds are lost. The impact includes potential loss of user funds, as the contract proceeds with state changes regardless of whether the underlying transfer succeeded, violating expected financial integrity.

findings.title: Bad implementation of storage management
findings.description: The contract uses a fixed storage cost constant (STORAGE_ADD_MARKET_DATA) of 859 bytes, but the add_bid() function allows bids to accumulate without sufficient storage checks, potentially causing market data to exceed the allocated size. The cause is the lack of dynamic storage validation or adjustment when adding new bids. An attacker could exploit this by repeatedly adding bids to inflate storage usage, eventually making it impossible to modify or remove data. The impact is that user funds may become locked if the contract cannot process further operations due to storage limits, disrupting normal marketplace functionality.

findings.title: Not enough funds for a transfer
findings.description: In the buy(), internal_accept_offer_series(), and internal_accept_offer() functions, when the user attaches exactly the required price, 1 yoctoNEAR is used for NFT transfer, leaving insufficient balance for the treasury fee transfer. The cause is the failure to account for the 1 yoctoNEAR used in the NFT transfer when validating the attached deposit. An attacker could exploit this by initiating purchases with exact amounts, causing the treasury to not receive its fee due to insufficient remaining balance. The impact is that the treasury may not receive rightful fees, leading to revenue loss and potential inconsistencies in fund distribution.

findings.title: Unlimited fee amount
findings.description: The set_transaction_fee() function allows the admin to set a transaction fee up to 10,000 basis points (100%), which could be abused to extract excessive fees from users. The cause is the lack of a reasonable upper limit on the fee percentage, despite input validation preventing values above 10,000. An attacker with admin privileges could exploit this by setting an unreasonably high fee, such as 99%, leading to user exploitation. The impact includes potential loss of user funds through excessive fees and reduced platform usability, damaging trust and adoption.

findings.title: Treasury fee won’t be transferred
findings.description: In resolve_purchase() and resolve_offer(), if the payout does not include the owner_id, the treasury fee is never transferred because the transfer logic is nested under the owner_id condition. The cause is flawed control flow where treasury fee transfer is only executed when the owner receives funds. An attacker could exploit this by structuring a payout that excludes the owner, preventing the treasury from receiving its fee. The impact is that the treasury may miss out on expected revenue, leading to financial discrepancies and potential governance issues.

findings.title: Division before multiplication
findings.description: The contract performs division before multiplication in several arithmetic operations (e.g., price calculations), which in integer math can lead to precision loss and incorrect results. The cause is improper ordering of arithmetic operations, particularly in time-based price decay and bid increment logic. An attacker could exploit this by triggering edge-case calculations where rounding errors accumulate, leading to unfair pricing or incorrect bid validations. The impact includes potential financial loss due to miscalculated prices or fees, undermining the fairness and correctness of the marketplace.

findings.title: Transaction fee view method
findings.description: The get_transaction_fee() function returns the current fee without checking if a scheduled fee update has taken effect, potentially returning outdated values. The cause is the lack of logic to evaluate the current timestamp against the start_time of a new fee. An attacker could exploit this by relying on stale fee data to manipulate transactions or mislead users. The impact is inconsistent fee application and potential confusion in transaction pricing, affecting transparency and user trust.

findings.title: Accept bids for ended auctions
findings.description: The accept_bid() function allows the contract owner to accept bids even after an auction has ended, which contradicts standard auction behavior. The cause is the conditional logic that permits owner intervention post-auction. An attacker with owner privileges could exploit this to unfairly accept late bids, disadvantaging legitimate bidders. The impact includes unfair transaction outcomes and potential disputes over NFT ownership, undermining auction integrity.

findings.title: Doesn’t check length of payout
findings.description: The contract does not validate the length of the payout structure received from NFT contracts, which can lead to excessive gas consumption or potential denial-of-service. The cause is the absence of a check against max_len_payout as required by NEP-199. An attacker could exploit this by returning an abnormally long payout list, forcing the contract to iterate unnecessarily. The impact is increased gas costs and potential transaction failure due to gas limits, degrading system performance.

findings.title: No checked math used
findings.description: In the storage_withdraw() function, unsigned integer arithmetic is used without overflow/underflow checks, which could lead to arithmetic errors if the amount exceeds available balance. The cause is the use of raw arithmetic operations instead of safe math libraries. An attacker could exploit this by crafting a withdrawal that causes integer overflow, potentially leading to incorrect balance updates. The impact includes potential loss of funds or incorrect state changes due to arithmetic errors.

findings.title: Typos and comments
findings.description: The code contains typographical errors such as 'DELIMETER' instead of 'DELIMITER' and inconsistent comments, such as referencing removal at length > 50 when the code checks for >= 100. The cause is lack of code review and attention to detail. While not directly exploitable, these issues reduce code readability and maintainability. The impact is increased risk of developer misunderstanding during future updates, potentially leading to logic errors or security flaws in subsequent changes.

findings.title: No checks for promise results with transfer native tokens
findings.description: The contract performs native token transfers via promises but does not verify their execution results. The cause is the absence of promise result handling mechanisms. An attacker could exploit this by deploying a contract that rejects incoming transfers, causing funds to be lost without detection. The impact includes potential loss of funds due to unverified transfers, reducing the reliability of financial operations.

findings.title: Remainder in NFT contracts
findings.description: According to NEP-199, financial contracts should subtract their commission before calling nft_transfer_payout with the remainder, but this contract does not follow that pattern. The cause is non-compliance with the standard royalty payout flow. An attacker could exploit this deviation to manipulate payout distributions or create inconsistencies in royalty payments. The impact is non-standard behavior that may lead to incorrect fund distribution and interoperability issues with other NEP-199 compliant contracts.
